For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{7}{18}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields $$

["question-f93ed602-5802-58b3-b8ce-1b9e0f1d7153" :question/worked-solution "Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & ↔{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{7}{18}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$"] ["question-f93ed602-5802-58b3-b8ce-1b9e0f1d7153" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-aeb22a13-5f92-563c-bd00-38953af464b9" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 & 6 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 6 & -18 & -12\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 & 6 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 6 & -18 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & -18 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $2$ non-pivot columns (the $2$nd and $3$rd ones). Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=2.
$$"] ["question-aeb22a13-5f92-563c-bd00-38953af464b9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e00646f1-87a0-5a44-9d32-d7268a416e97" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-32b7b7cc-73cb-5678-9200-bd4242fb8265" :question/worked-solution "Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y+z.
$$

  

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}-2y+z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,y,z\in R}.$"] ["question-32b7b7cc-73cb-5678-9200-bd4242fb8265" :question/difficulty :tutorial/content "The **kernel** of a linear transformation is the set of vectors that map to the zero vector. We define it formally as follows:

> *For a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$, the **kernel** of $\mathbf{T}$ is the set of all the vectors $\mathbf{u}$ such that $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.$ We can write this as*
> 
> 
> $$
> \textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) = \left\{ \;\mathbf{u} \;| \; \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0} \right\}.
> $$

The diagram below shows the kernel of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}: V \rightarrow V$ in a vector space $V$.

![](images/05/05f8c544d55c6bb07e4063150e586f8b4a7c51a352c2ff8ddda8c4cd5047dd93.png)

Notice that, because of linearity, the zero vector is always in the kernel of a linear transformation: 

$$
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{T}(0\cdot\mathbf{v})=0\cdot\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})= \mathbf 0
$$

for any vector $\mathbf{v}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "50e4315c-9517-5360-820c-0b5ac6318f72" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3529 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.

A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction.
